To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The amount of dissolved organic carbon available for planktonic bacterioplankton in oligotrophic lake waters is correlated with the amount and type of humic matter in the water.

the amount of dissolved organic carbon consumed by bacterioplankton in dilution cultures was the same in all lakes (average = 9.5% of the total DOC, coefficient of variation = 24%), and that the amount of DOC consumed was the same fraction of that available to bacteria (average = 0.25%, coefficient of variation =28%).

the total DOC pool of humic lakes was more available for bacteria than that of clearwater lakes, and that the fraction of the total available DOC pool that was consumed by the bacteria was the same in all lakes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how humic substances affect the bacterial production and the bacterial carbon flow through the planktonic food web of oligotrophic lakes.
the availability of DOC for planktonic bacterioplankton and with its relevance for the structure of the planktonic food web in humic and clear-water lakes.
the role of dissolved organic matter as a substrate for bacteria in lakes, and the consequences of this role for the structure and function of aquatic ecosystems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DOC pool of humic lakes is available for planktonic bacterial growth, but that the humic matter in the DOC pool does not support a higher bacterial growth than in clearwater lakes.
humic substances, in contrast to DOC, do not support bacterial production, at least not in the oligotrophic lakes studied.
the bacterial biomass is positively correlated with the DOC pool, and that the bacterial growth efficiency is independent of the DOC pool size.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
planktonic bacteria are capable of using the same fraction of humic DOC as of DOC in clearwater lakes and that the humic DOC is not a limiting resource in oligotrophic waters.
planktonic bacteria are not limited by humic matter in oligotrophic humic lakes.
the bacterial biomass and production in oligotrophic clearwater and humic lakes are determined by the same factors, namely, the availability of DOC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
humic lakes can support a higher bacterial standing stock than clearwater lakes, because they contain a larger pool of dissolved organic carbon, which is a substrate for bacteria.
humic lakes can support a higher bacterial production than clearwater lakes because they have a larger pool of organic carbon available for bacterial growth.

the amount of DOC available for bacterial growth is not a limiting factor for bacterial biomass in humic lakes, and that bacterial production and growth efficiency are similar to those observed in clearwater lakes.
